Interfaces 2022, 14, 46457−46470 Read Online ACCESS Metrics & More Article Recommendations * sı Supporting Information ABSTRACT: Due to the poor electronic conductivity of solid sulfur and sulfides, the dissolution of Sα−(α = 0, 2/8, 2/6, 2/4) into a liquid electrolyte and the vehicular diffusion of Sα−to carbon black are necessary for the electrochemical activity of a sulfur cathode in lithium-sulfur (Li-S) batteries.

However, exactly how much dissolution and diffusion are required for high sulfur utilization and how this may control the minimum electrolyte/sulfur ratio, (E/S)min, have not been quantitatively settled.

In this work, we show experimentally that a dissolved polysulfide concentration which is too high (>10−20 MS) may gel the liquid electrolyte, leading to catastrophic loss of Sα−mobility, a failure mode that is especially susceptible in a high-donor-number (DN) electrolyte under a lean condition (low E/S), similar to a traffic jam, resulting in high electrochemical polarization and low sulfur utilization.

In contrast, we show that a low-DN electrolyte, even with a low polysulfide solubility of 0.1−0.5 MS, will never encounter a gelation catastrophe even at extremely low E/S, leading to unprecedentedly high energy density.

Specifically, high sulfur utilizations of 96% (1600 mAh g−1) and 78% (1300 mAh g−1) are reached in an electrolyte as lean as E/S = 2 and 1 μL mg−1 Li-S coin cells when DME1.6LiFSI-HFE of low solvation capability (DN = 13.9) is adopted, even paired against a high-sulfur-loading cathode (5 mg cm−2).

KEYWORDS: lithium-sulfur battery, electrolyte/sulfur ratio, gelation, high sulfur utilization, gravimetric energy density ■INTRODUCTION Lithium-sulfur (Li-S) is a promising post-lithium-ion battery chemistry due to the high theoretical energy density (2600 Wh kg−1, based on the active electrode materials of lithium and sulfur)1−3 and low price (the price of sulfur is US$0.1 kg−1).4,5 While Li-S chemistry is very attractive in applications where gravimetric energy density matters a great deal, it confronts great challenges in coming to the realization of the high actual energy density on a full-cell level.6−10 One of the most emerging concerns is the low sulfur utilization under a lean electrolyte condition (the electrolyte condition in a Li-S battery can be described by the electrolyte/sulfur ratio, E/S, which is the total volume of injected liquid electrolyte to the total weight of sulfur in the cell, in units of μL mg−1; a lean electrolyte condition means low E/S).
The E/S currently used in Li-S batteries is usually larger than 5 μL mg−1 to boost the sulfur utilization.
This means that the inactive liquid electrolyte weighs several times more than the active sulfur.

The exact reason why such a high E/S was required has never been clearly explained in the literature, but what researchers have found experimentally was that when the E/S ratio was reduced to 2 μL mg−1, high polarization is always observed at the end of the first discharging plateau in the Li-S battery, accompanied by the absence of the second discharging plateau and thus low sulfur utilization (as shown in Figure S1).11 Theoretically, due to the poor electronic conductivity of solid sulfur and sulfides, the operation of a sulfur cathode relies on local sulfur mobility (LSM), which means that solid insulating sulfur species first dissolve into the liquid electrolyte and subsequently diffuse to the nearest conductive carbon black to access free electrons and to perform redox reactions, as shown in Figure 1a.12,13 Therefore, the dissolution and vehicular diffusion of Sα−(α = 0, 2/8, 2/6, 2/4) are two key steps for the electrochemical activity of the sulfur cathode.

The dissolution of polysulfides can stimulate the LSM to promote the electrochemical kinetics of the sulfur cathode, but it can also cause global sulfur mobility (GSM), which is the movement of active substances between positive and negative electrodes, leading to the loss of active substances and the polysulfide shuttle effect.
Therefore, a proper amount of dissolution and diffusion is vital to achieve a high sulfur utilization, which fortunately can be optimized by adjusting the E/S ratio.

To make the ensuing discussions easier, we will use MS ≡mol(Sα−) L−1 as the unit of dissolution: that is, the number of moles of Sα−dissolved in 1 L of the liquid solution phase (e.g., if the solubility of Li2S8 is 1 M L−1 then the dissolution of S1/4−is 8 MS).

Based on the thermodynamic reaction equilibrium, the MS value in an actual cell should depend on the intrinsic electrolyte solvation capability as well as E/S, especially in a high-DN electrolyte.

For example, with an unrealistically high E/S such as 10 μL mg−1 of DOL+DME, which is unfortunately frequently used in academic research and the literature, the maximum MS value in an actual cell during cycling may be around 5 MS, very high but not yet problematic.

However, when E/S = 3 μL mg−1 of the same electrolyte is used, the maximum MS value in an actual cell during cycling will skyrocket to beyond 10−15 MS, which could be highly problematic for the cell, as we will demonstrate.

One school of thought why this is necessary is the “complete dissolution theory”: that is, the complete dissolution of polysulfides into the liquid electrolyte at some point in the discharge and charge is a necessary condition for the Li-S battery to cycle.

According to this school of thought, high polarization in a lean electrolyte Li-S battery can be attributed to the incomplete dissolution of polysulfide:11,14,15 that is, some polysulfides are dissolved as Sα−(electrolyte), while others remain as solid-phase Li2Sn (α = 2/n).

For example, the solubility of Li2S8 was reported to be 6−7 MS in a common ether-solvent electrolyte, and assuming all sulfur inventory in the cathode must exist as dissolved Sα−(α = 2/8) in the first discharge plateau and no solid sulfur inventory exists at that point, this would require the minimum electrolyte amount to be (E/S)min = 4−5 μL/mg.15 When the E/S ratio is lower than 4−5 μL mg−1, the “complete dissolution theory” would say Li2S8 generated in the battery discharge would exceed the solubility limit and precipitate out as a solid phase, which somehow will block the conduction pathways and result in high polarization.14−16 Nazar et al.17,18 have reported that a Li- S battery could also deliver high sulfur utilization in a sparingly solvated electrolyte (SSE), which has very small solubility for Li2Sn.
The solubility of Li2Sn in an SSE was estimated to be less than 3 wt % in a cell, which means that 97 wt % of the polysulfides cannot dissolve and act as a solid phase during the battery operation.

The normal operation of the Li-S battery in an SSE indicates that the complete dissolution of polysulfides at some point is not a necessary condition for a Li-S battery to cycle, which contradicts the complete dissolution theory.

Therefore, the enlarged polarization in the lean electrolyte Li-S battery may not necessarily becaused by the incomplete dissolution of polysulfides and the failure of the battery under a lean-electrolyte condition might be the outcome of multiple causes.

Instead, we show experimentally in this work that the high dissolution of polysulfides (e.g., 30 MS) in ether-solvent electrolyte is responsible for the high polarization in the leanelectrolyte Li-S battery.

We found that the reported solubility of Li2S8 (6−7 MS) in the literature mainly comes from the test results of coin cells through a dilution approach and may not be accurate.19,20 The total amount of electrolyte added in cells often cannot be completely absorbed by the positive electrode due to the existence of a large number of head spaces, and the fraction of electrolyte that can actually participate in the dissolution of polysulfide is often much smaller.

An electrolyte with high solvation capability (high donor number, DN) contributes to high polysulfide solubility and makes it easy to gel the electrolyte under a lean condition because of the reachable super high concentration.
In contrast, an electrolyte with a low solvation capability (low DN) contributes to the low solubility of polysulfides and can avoid the gelation of the electrolyte even at an extremely low E/S.

The unexpectedly high solubility limit means that the solid Li2Sn can indeed mostly dissolve into the liquid electrolyte, Li2Sn(solid) →2Li+(liquid) + nSα−(liquid), even under condition as lean as E/S ≤1 μL mg−1 (if the Li2S8 completely dissolves, E/S = 1 μL mg−1 corresponds to 31.2 MS).
However, a value greater than 10 MS is not a good thing.

In other words, when E/S sweeps from the flooded condition (e.g., 5 μL mg−1) to the lean condition (e.g., 1 μL mg−1), the actual concentration of Sα−in the liquid electrolyte will skyrocket and can become super highly concentrated (∼30 MS) or even reach the electrolyte gelation point (∼60 MS) under an ultralean condition (E/S ≤1 μL mg−1).
When this occurs, the mobility of Sα−in the liquid electrolyte will experience a catastrophic loss due to the sharp increased viscosity, as as shown in the schematic in Figure 1d.

A frozen Sα−transport, due to ironically too much dissolved Sα−, is definitely undesirable for the electrochemical activity of the sulfur cathode because the Sα−jammed in the electrolyte cannot reach the carbon black to access free electrons and perform redox reactions (see Figure 1b).
We have shown in this work that this is the typical failure mode in a leanelectrolyte Li-S battery with a high-donor-number (DN) electrolyte.

To better interpret the relationship between the concentration and the mobility of Sα−, we can envision the cars in a traffic jam, all of which show almost no mobility at high concentration.21,22 Up to now, few methods have been available to improve the sulfur utilization under a lean-electrolyte condition.
Especially, a high-sulfur-utilization Li-S battery under an ultraleanelectrolyte condition (e.g., E/S = 1 μL mg−1) has not yet been reported.
Herein, we show that a high dissolution of polysulfides >5 MS is definitely overkill and unnecessary to reach high sulfur utilization.
Rather, reducing the solubility limit is an effective way to improve the Li-S battery performance under a lean-electrolyte condition.

According to Faraday’s law, Q = nzF, we show that only 0.1 MS Sα− solubility can sustain a 0.5C current density in a Li-S battery while 0.5 MS solubility can sustain over 2C current density, even under a lean condition of E/S = 1 μL mg−1, as shown in Figure S2.

This means that a 0.1−0.5 MS solubility limit, far different from the 5−60 MS we have in an ether-based electrolyte, is already sufficient to sustain a high electrochemical activity of the sulfur cathode.

Philosophically this makes sense, since we know 1 M Li salt is sufficient to support long-range Li+ transport in all kinds of batteries; thus, in order to support local sulfur mobility (LSM) while cutting down global sulfur mobility (GSM),12,13 one should not need much more than 1 MS for Sα−!

This consideration paints a different conceptual picture from the “complete dissolution theory” and points to a very different optimal MS-parametric regime (less than 1 MS, rather than >5 MS) for the liquid electrolyte design for a Li-S battery.

Most importantly, by cutting down the intrinsic solubility limit, there is never complete dissolution at any point, and in fact most of the sulfur and sulfides are in the form of Li2Sn(solid) and only a small fraction is in the form of Sα−(liquid) in the electrolyte, and so the liquid electrolyte will never encounter a gelation catastrophe even at an extremely low E/S.
Quantitatively, the optimum [Sα−(liquid)] might be around 0.5 MS to support LSM, and this value is far from the electrolyte gelation point (>30 MS).

By preserving the mobility of Sα−under a lean condition (Figure 1d), which can only move by vehicular diffusion and not by a Grotthusslike exchange mechanism like H+/Li+, one can thus achieve an unprecedentedly low (E/S)min and a high energy density of the Li-S battery.
In this work, through adopting the sparingly solvated electrolyte DME1.6LiFSI-HFE with a low DN of 13.9, the dissolution of polysulfides was suppressed to an extremely low level.

As a result, high sulfur utilizations of 96% (1600 mAh g−1) and 78% (1300 mAh g−1) in lean electrolytes with E/S = 2 and 1 μL mg−1 Li-S coin cells (tested at room temperature) have been reached, even paired against a highsulfur-loading cathode (5 mg cm−2).

Combining with the highsulfur-loading cathode we developed in the previous work,23 a 2.3 Ah Li-S pouch cell assembled with industrially satisfactory parameters (sulfur loading 7 mg cm−2, E/S = 1 μL mg−1, 1× lithium excess) was demonstrated; it turns out that the practical energy density can reach 589 Wh kg−1. ■EXPERIMENTAL SECTION Material and Electrolyte Preparation.

S8 and Li2S were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich with a purity of 99.9%. 1,2- Dimethoxyethane (DME), 1,3-dioxolane (DOL), lithium bis- (trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (LiTFSI), and lithium bis- (fluorosulfonyl)imide (LiFSI) were purchased from DodoChem (Suzhou, China) with a water content of less than 50 ppm.
The electrolytes and Li2Sn solutions were prepared in a glovebox with water content and oxygen contents of less than 0.1 ppm (MIKROUNA, Super 1220/750).

The electrolytes at different concentrations were prepared by changing the molar ratio between lithium salts and solvents (from 1:9 to 1:1.6). 1,1,2,2-Tetrafluoroethyl-2,2,3,3-tetrafluoropropyl ether (HFE) was added to highly concentrated electrolytes of (DME)3Li salts and (DME)1.6Li salts at a volume ratio of 2:1.
Li2Sn solutions at different S concentrations were prepared by mixing stoichiometric Li2S and S8 by an evaporation method.
First, a dilute Li2Sn solution (no precipitates at the beginning) was obtained by mixing stoichiometric Li2S and S8 in excess solvent (E/S = 10 μL mg−1, 3.12 MS).
After a full reaction, the homogeneous dilute solution was then evaporated gradually until a solid phase started to appear.
The immediate concentration was recorded as the solubility of Li2Sn.
Solubility Test of Li2S8.
In the evaporation method, a dilute Li2S8 solution was first obtained by mixing stoichiometric Li2S and S8 in DME (the E/S in Li2S8 was controlled at 10 μL mg−1 corresponding to 3.12 MS L−1).
After that, the Li2S8 solution was stirred at 60 °C for 10 h to accelerate the reaction.
Finally, the solution was evaporated at 60 °C to reach the target concentration by monitoring the variation of the solvent weight.
In a test of the Li2S4 solubility, the Li2S and S8 could not react adequately, even after stirring at 80 °C for 1 week at a high E/S of 20 μL mg−1 (1.56 MS).
Construction of a Transparent Capillary Li-S Battery (C- LSB).
The C-LSB was constructed based on a square quartz capillary tube with a size of 0.4 mm × 0.4 mm × 15 mm.

The cathode current collector (carbon-coated aluminum foil) was cut into long strips (0.3 mm × 5 mm) in advance, and one end was coated with a cathode slurry (the slurry area was controlled at 0.3 mm × 0.3 mm and with a sulfur loading of 1.5 mg cm−2).
Similarly, the lithium metal anode was cut into long strips with a size of 0.3 mm × 5 mm in advance.
When the battery was assembled, the lithium anode and sulfur cathode were inserted from both ends of the quartz capillary and the conductive wires were led out, respectively.
The electrolyte was injected by using a microinjector, and the electrolyte volume was about 2.4 μL (the E/S ratio in C-LSB was about 1700 μL mg−1).
The ends of the capillary were sealed with AB glue.
A combination of an optical microscope and some other methods of spectral analysis of C-LSB enabled us to study the electrochemical process of the sulfur cathode in situ in the battery operation.

Sulfur Cathode Manufacturing.
Sulfur cathodes with a high sulfur loading (5 mg cm−2 for coin cells and 7 mg cm−2 for pouch cells) were fabricated by a lyophilization method, as we reported previously.
First, commercial sulfur powder and Ketjen black (KB) (Lion Co., ECP-600JD) were mixed uniformly in a ratio of 4:1 and heated at 155 °C for 12 h (80 wt % sulfur).

After that, the as-prepared S/KB composites were mixed with KB and aqueous LA-133 binder (Chengdu Indigo Power Sources Co., Ltd., China) at mass ratios of 80:15:5 (5 mg cm−2) and 90:5:5 (7 mg cm−2) to reach uniform slurries.
Thereafter, the slurry was coated onto an aluminum foil current collector at different thicknesses according to the sulfur loading.

The as-prepared electrode was first frozen at −40 °C for 2 h and then vacuumed to 0.1 Pa for 2 h to induce ice crystal sublimation and finally compacted to the target thickness and porosity (the porosity of the sulfur cathode was controlled at 55%; the thickness of the 5 mg cm−2 cathode was 85 μm and the compact density was 0.6 g S cm−3 and the thickness of the 7 mg cm−2 cathode was 105 μm and the compact density was 0.66 g S cm−3).
A sulfur cathode with low sulfur loading (1.5 mg cm−2) was also fabricated to assemble a C-LSB.
The sulfur cathode was fabricated by conventional thermal drying with the same sulfur ratio as in the 7 mg cm−2 sulfur cathode.

Ltd., Shanghai, China). ■RESULTS WITH DISCUSSION Electrolyte Gelation under Lean Conditions.

Previously, the solubility of Li2Sn in the commonly used DOL +DME electrolyte was reported to be 6−7 MS (based on Li2S8) through a dilution test approach, where an extra amount of stoichiometric Li2S and S8 was added to the solvents, followed by a certain period of stirring (typically at 60 °C for 10 h), and then the saturated solution was diluted gradually until all species were dissolved.19,20 In this case, the solubility based on Li2S8 could be calculated with the total added solvent amount and the Li2S8 molarity according to Li2S + 7 8S8 → Li2S8.
Note that such a dilution approach assumes that Li2S and S8 react completely in the first place and the only undissolved species is Li2S8, which, however, is not necessarily true.
As a matter of fact, we examined the precipitates in the “saturated solution” by preparing concentrated Li2S8 in DME (15.6 MS, corresponding to E/S = 2 μL mg−1).
After stirring at 60 °C for 10 h, there are still a large amount of precipitate in the bottom of the bottle, as shown in Figure S3a.

The Raman spectrum and XRD analysis (Figure S3b,c) indicate that the precipitates mainly consist of S8, with a small part being Li2S, which is consistent with the weight percent of S8 and Li2S used to reach Li2S8 (∼7:1).

That is, the solubility of polysulfides may be larger than 6−7 MS because the chemical reaction between Li2S and S8 is actually not complete at high concentration; we adopted an evaporation method to test the solubility in this study, which is more widely applied in solubility tests to obtain a more accurate solubility of Li2Sn.

As shown in Figure 2a, a dilute Li2Sn solution (no precipitates at the beginning) was first obtained by mixing stoichiometric Li2S and S8 in excess solvent (e.g., E/S = 10 μL mg−1, 3.12 MS); after a full reaction, a homogeneous dilute solution was then evaporated gradually until solid-phase Li2Sn started to appear.
The immediate concentration was recorded as the solubility of Li2Sn.
Surprisingly, we found that the solubility of Li2S8 is far more than 6−7 MS.
Figure S4b and Figure 2b,c show the optical microscopy images (500× magnification) of DME with different concentrations of Li2S8.
These images were obtained by absorbing the electrolyte in a capillary tube and then observing through an optical microscope, as schematically shown in Figure S4a.

This indicated that no solid precipitates were found in the 10.4 MS (Figure S4b) and 15.6 MS (Figure 2b) electrolytes, even though the current Li2S8 concentrations of which in DME have exceeded those commonly reported.
As we further evaporated the solvents to 31.2 MS (corresponding to E/S = 1 μL mg−1), the electrolyte mixture became slurrylike with precipitates showing up, as revealed in Figure 2c.
However, a Raman spectral analysis identified these precipitates as elemental S8 instead of Li2S8 (Figure S5).

The generation of S8 may be attribute to the disproportionation reaction Li2S8 →S8 + Li2S6/Li2S4/Li2S2, which was reported to be exacerbated at high Li2S8 concentration.24 Therefore, while it might be difficult to evaluate the solubility of Li2S8 exactly, one could conclude that the solubility of Li2S8 must be greaater than 6−7 MS and may exceed 31.2 MS because no solid Li2S8 precipitated in the 31.2 MS electrolyte.
The above means that, chemically, ethers really prefer to mix with sulfides.
Particular attention should be paid to the viscosity evolution of the electrolyte as the concentration of Li2S8 increases, and importantly, it is directly related to the vehicular diffusion of Sn 2−.
From the inset in Figure 2c, the electrolyte has become quite sticky and could be drawn into a long line at 31.2 MS, indicating a high viscosity.

The red line in Figure 2e quantitatively shows that the viscosity of the electrolyte has increased about 3 orders of magnitude from 4.3 to 1.8 × 103 mPa s when the polysulfide concentration increases from 6.24 to 31.2 MS (the viscosity was tested in a rheometer with its rotation mode at 25 °C, and the value of the viscosity was chosen at a shear rate of 500 s−1).
Meanwhile, Figure S6 shows that the electrolyte has changed from a Newtonian fluid to a non-Newtonian fluid when the concentration is increased to 31.2 MS.

To make it even worse, as shown in Figure 2d, when the concentration of Li2S8 is increased to 62.4 MS (E/S = 0.5 μL mg−1; the mole ratio of DME to nominal Li2S8 is about 1.2:1), the electrolyte transforms from a liquid (with fairly good fluidity despite the high viscosity) to a sulfur gel with barely any flowability that behaves like a solid.

As a result, the viscosity of the electrolyte has further increased to 1.0 × 107 mPa s (the viscosity was tested in a rheometer with its oscillation mode, and the viscosity used here is the complex viscosity, as shown in Figure S7).
According to the Stokes−Einstein relation = r 1 6 for vehicular diffusion, where r represents the ionic radius and the mobility of ions (μ) is in reverse proportion with media viscosity (η).
The increased viscosity of the electrolyte definitely leads to low vehicular diffusion of Sn 2−and Li+.

The black line in Figure 2e shows that the conductivity of electrolytes has decreased from 3.88 to 6.03 × 10−3 mS cm−1 when the concentration of Li2S8 increased from 6.24 to 62.4 MS (the conductivity of liquid electrolyte was tested with a conductivity meter, and the conductivity of the sulfur gel was tested by an EIS impendence method, as shown in Figure S8).
Despite the decrease in conductivity, the lithium ions can still be transported because of the small ion radius (0.076 nm) and possibility of a Grotthuss-like collective exchange mechanism.
However, the diffusion of Sn 2−would be very difficult due to the larger radius (0.4−0.8 nm) when the viscosity has skyrocketed.
Figure S7 also shows that the elastic modulus and viscosity modulus of the sulfur gel reach 66.35 and 20.29 MPa, respectively, at room temperature (25 °C).
A similar elastomeric feature was also found in DME containing 1 M LiTFSI at the same E/S ratio (E/S = 0.5 μL mg−1) (Figure S9).
The yellowish color in Figure S9 may result from the exacerbated disproportionation of Li2S8 to form S8 due to the increased concentration of lithium ions.

Therefore, we speculate that the gelation of the electrolyte initiated by the high Li2Sn concentration is the reason for the extremely high polarization of the Li-S battery under a lean electrolyte condition because of the sharp decrease of Sn 2−mobility.

To comprehensively understand the gelation transition, we conducted a constituent analysis of the electrolytes at different Li2S8 concentrations through Raman spectrometry, as demonstrated in Figure 2f.

Based on the results above, we conclude that the gelation of the electrolyte is easily initiated under a lean condition and Area 2 in Figure 3b is sulfur gel.

Actually, when out the XPS experiment is carried out, it takes more than 48 h to vacuum the sample, reflecting that there are solvents (DME) in the sulfur gel that are strongly bonded and thus quite difficult to pump out due to the strong interaction between the solvent and polysulfides (perhaps a coordinate covalent bond between ether oxygen and Li+).
The peak at 164.3 eV indicates there is still S8 in the cathode, which may be attributed to the unreacted S8 and/or the disproportionation of metastable polysulfides (e.g., Li2S8 → Li2S6/4 + S8).

Based on the results above, we conclude that the gelation of electrolyte is easily initiated under a lean condition and should be responsible for the enlarged polarization in the Li-S battery.
Note that in the real Li-S battery the gelation of the electrolyte may not be initiated by only one kind of lithium polysulfide (e.g., Li2S8).
Instead, there is a high possibility that the gelation of electrolytes may be initiated by several kinds of Li2Sn at the same time, including Li2S8, Li2S6, and Li2S4.
As a matter of fact, in a failed Li-S battery, the greatest polarization in the discharge process often occurs at the position where Li2S4 starts to appear (see Figure S2b,c).
Thus, we speculate that lithium polysulfides containing Li2S4 may be more potent in gelling electrolytes.

In the previous section, we concluded that the gelation of the electrolyte initiated by the high dissolution of Li2Sn was the main reason for the enlarged polarization in the leanelectrolyte Li-S battery.

As a verification, in the following sections, we prepared an electrolyte with low solvation capability to suppress the dissolution of Li2Sn and to study the electrochemical performance of a lean-electrolyte Li-S battery.
Generally speaking, the solubility of polysulfides is determined by the solvation capability of electrolytes.

In this work, electrolytes with low solvation capabilities were reached by regulating the concentration of lithium salts, as reported previously.27−29 The lithium salt used in our experiment is lithium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (LiFSI), and the solvent is DME, both of which are reported to have great compatibility with the lithium metal anode.28Figure 4a shows the Raman spectra of electrolytes with different LiFSI concentrations.

The peaks located at 1138 and 1123 cm−1 are respectively correlated to the asymmetric stretching mode of C−O−C (νas(C−O)) in DME before and after coordination with Li+.30,31 Commonly, the content of the free solvents in the electrolyte is an important index of the solvation capability that can be reflected by the intensity of the Raman peaks.

It can be found that the ratio between the coordinated DME and free DME increases rapidly along with the increment of LiFSI concentration, as indicated by the variation of the peak intensity at 1123 and 1138 cm−1.
In particular, when the concentration of LiFSI exceeds 3.2 M ((DME)3LiFSI), the original peak at 1138 cm−1 has disappeared, suggesting that most of the free DME solvents are complexing with Li+.

Nazar et al. have achieved dendrite-free lithium plating of the electrolyte at a E/S ratio of 5 μL mg−1 by using a diglyme electrolyte with a saturated LiTFSI salt, G2:LiTFSI (0.8:1), to adjust the electrolyte network structure.22 As a comparison, we also studied the Raman spectra of electrolytes adopting lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (LiTFSI) as the salt, shown in Figure 4b.

From Figure 4b we find that LiTFSI is not good at lowering the electrolyte solvation capability, as typically there are still a large number of free DME molecules in the electrolyte even when the concentration of LiTFSI is increased to 6 M ((DME)1.6LiTFSI, approaching the saturation concentration of LiTFSI in DME).

The high content of the free DME in the LiTFSI-based electrolyte makes it incapable of suppressing the dissolution of Li2Sn effectively, which also results in electrolyte gelation under leanelectrolyte conditions.

The reason for such a contrast in coordinating DME with the LiFSI salt may be attributed to the smaller bonding energies between Li+ and FSI−, and thus DME can easily participate in the solvation shell and coordinate with Li+, rendering less free DME.

On the other hand, the intensifying coordination environment of Li+ with TFSI−in the LiTFSI-based electrolyte makes TFSI−more likely to participate in the solvation shell, resulting in less DME coordination with Li+ and concomitantly more free DME.32 Figure 4.

The donor number (DN) is often a measure of the ability of a solvent to solvate cations.
Herein, to describe the depressed solvation capability more quantitatively, we develop a donor number (DN) testing method to study the solvation capability of electrolytes.

The testing method of DN was referred to a study by Hahn et al.,33 who adopted standard proton (1H) NMR with chloroform (CHCl3) as the reference acceptor to establish a correlation between the CHCl3 1H NMR shift and the solvent donor number.

The theoretical basis is that the molecular interaction between chloroform and the solvent would decrease the electron shielding at the hydrogen of chloroform when CHCl3 is added into donor solvents, and the shift of chloroform in donor solvents will be downfield of the shift of pure chloroform, since the acceptor hydrogen loses shielding.
The downfield shift (Δδ) increases with increasing DN and is more pronounced for a dilute solution wherein the isolated chloroform molecules are surrounded by solvent molecules.
In this study, we use this method to evaluate the DN of electrolytes with different lithium salts and lithium salt concentrations to describe the solvation capability of electrolyte quantitatively.
In detail, 0.1 M CHCl3 was added to the different electrolytes, and then we measured the chemical shift of 1H NMR (δ(1H)) of CHCl3.
Figure S13a shows that δ(1H) in pure CHCl3 is 7.29 ppm.
Figure 4c shows the δ(1H) values of CHCl3 in the different electrolytes and the corresponding Δδ values on comparison with the δ(1H) value in pure CHCl3.

It reveals a lower Δδ with an increasing LiFSI concentration, indicating a smaller decrease of the electron shielding at the hydrogen of chloroform, which reflects the lower electrondonating ability and solvation capability.
The NMR testing results are consistent with the Raman spectrum results shown in Figure 4a.
To describe the solvation capability of electrolyte quantitatively, we give a simple correction between the Δδ and DN, DN = λΔδ(CHCl3).
To obtain λ, we first tested the Δδ value of CHCl3 in pure DME solvent, which has a known DN (DN = 20), to determine the coefficient (see Figure S13b and Figure 4c) to be λ = 10.1.
Then, we calculated the DN of each electrolyte by using the formula DN = 10.1Δδ(CHCl3).

Figure 4d shows the DN of each electrolyte calculated by our method, from which it is obvious that LiFSI with high concentration leads to a low DN, and the lowest DN was achieved in DME1.6LiFSI with a value of 15.
Our method is more accurate and quantitative than Raman spectrometry results.
In Raman spectra (Figure 4a), DME3LiFSI and DME1.6LiFSI have the same spectra, making it difficult to determine the relatively greater (or smaller) solvation capability.
As a comparison, the DN of electrolytes with LiTFSI has also been tested in this work, as shown in Figure 4c,d.
Not surprisingly, the LiFSIbased electrolytes we used have a lower DN than LiTFSI-based electrolytes at each concentration, which is beneficial to suppress the dissolution of Li2Sn.
These electrolytes with different solvation capabilities will have different solubilities to Li2Sn, as we will show in the following.

It worth noting that we have developed a method to evaluate the solvation capability of electrolytes quantitatively, and the DN calculated in our work may not equal the DN tested by conventional calorimetry.

In Situ Study of the Lithium Polysulfide Dissolution.
To study polysulfide dissolution in different electrolytes, a transparent capillary Li-S battery (C-LSB) was developed in this work, as illustrated in Figure 5a.
A 2.4 μL portion of the electrolyte was injected in the C-LSB by using a microinjector, and therefore the E/S ratio is about 1700 μL mg−1.
Combined with an optical microscope, C-LSB enables us to observe the evolution of the electrolyte and sulfur cathode visually at different discharge stages, as shosn in Figure 5b.
Figure S15 shows the optical microscope images of the sulfur cathode in C-LSB before and after injecting electrolytes.

Interestingly, large numbers of white crystal particles at 101 μm size have formed on the surface of the sulfur cathode after immersion in a high-solvation-capability electrolyte ((DME)9LiFSI, DN = 18.3), as shown in Figure S15b.
Similar white particles were also found in (DME)9LiTFSI and 1 M LiTFSI/DOL+DME (Figure S15c,d).
A Raman spectrum study (Figure S15g) shows that the white particles are S8.

Figure S15e,f gives images of the sulfur cathode after immersion in the medium-solvationcapability electrolyte DME3LiFSI-HFE (DN = 14.9) and lowsolvation-capability electrolyte (DME)1.6LiFSI-HFE (DN = 13.9), respectively.
Obviously, the size and number of S8 particles formed on the cathode surface are reduced.
Even though the particular reason for the aggregation of S8 is not clear, it suggests that the formation of S8 is closely related to the electrolyte solvation capability.
Except for S8, this setup is also very effective in studying the dissolution of polysulfides.
Generally, the discharge process of a Li-S battery in common high-solvation-capability electrolytes can be divided into three stages, as shown in Figure 5b.
Herein, we studied the dissolution of polysulfides in the different discharge stages in C-LSB by observing the morphology and color of the electrolyte and sulfur cathode.
Figure 5c-e gives images of (DME)9LiFSI (DN = 18.3) and the sulfur cathode at the different discharge stages of the C-LSB.

From Figure 5c we can observe that significant dissolution of Li2S8/Li2S6 took place in stage I, as indicated by the golden color of the electrolyte, which represents the typical polysulfide dissolution situation in a Li-S battery.
When sulfur completely reacts, the color of the electrolyte becomes the deepest, which corresponds to the first voltage drop in the discharge curve shown in Figure 5b.

At stage II, different from the sufficient dissociation of Li2S8/Li2S6 at stage I, the color of the electrolyte gradually becomes lighter and cluster networks can be observed in the electrolyte, as emphasized in the white square, which also indicates that the Li2S8/Li2S6 gradually decreases (Figure 5d).
The polysulfide clusters in the electrolyte gradually disappear (Figure 5e) in stage III, indicating that this process corresponds to the transition of Li2S4 to solid Li2S2/Li2S.
Therefore, the solid in Figure 5d was determined to be a Li2S4 cluster.
This larger and larger colloidal network will serve as the structural skeleton of the gel, once the percolation threshold is reached.

The formation of the Li2S4 cluster may be attributed to the strong interaction between S4 2−and Li+, which is hard to dissociate sufficiently by the electrolyte.34 Note that the Li2S4 networks formed in the electrolyte may accelerate the electrolyte gelation under a lean condition because the cluster networks are more likely to link with each other to form 3D continuous networks.
The observation of Li2S4 cluster networks confirms what we have speculated in the previous section that polysulfides containing Li2S4 are more potent in gelling electrolytes.
Similar cluster networks were also found in the discharge process in (DME)9LiTFSI and 1 M LiTFSI/DOL+DME (see Figure S16a,b).
As the discharge goes into stage III, the cluster networks gradually disappear due to the conversion of Li2S4 to solid Li2S2/Li2S (Figure 5e).
Not surprisingly, Li2Sn shows a different dissolution situation when the solvation capability is reduced.

Figure 5f shows that the dissolution ofLi2S8/Li2S6 has been suppressed effectively in (DME)3LiFSI-HFE with a medium solvation capability (DN = 14.9), as indicated by the light color of the electrolyte.

Meanwhile, no Li2S4 clusters have been observed in discharge stage II (Figure 5g), implying that the solvation capability of the electrolyte has been depressed to a low level that fails to solvate Li2S4.

However, it is worth noting that the color of the electrolyte does not fade as the discharge continues and keeps the flaxen color to stage III (Figure 5h), which is different from the observation in (DME)9LiFSI.

The persistent color in (DME)3LiFSI-HFE indicates that the solubilized S8 2−/S6 2−in the electrolyte has difficulty in diffusing back to the sulfur cathode, which may be attributed to the complex solvation structure in highconcentration electrolyte.35 Note that there is still obvious dissolution of Li2S8/Li2S6 in (DME)3LiFSI-HFE despite the fact that the DN (solvation capability) has been reduced from 18.3 to 14.9.

Herein, we provide a simple method to identify the solvation capability of electrolytes.
We find that the electrolyte’s solvation capability is related to the reduction potential of S8 to Li2S8 in the discharge process of the Li-S battery.
Therefore, the reduction peak can be used to evaluate the solvation capability of electrolytes.
Figure 6g shows the discharge dQ/dV curves of the Li-S battery, from which we can see that the electrolytes with higher solvation capability lead to a higher reduction potential.
The reduction peaks of (DME)9LiFSI, (DME)3LiFSI-HFE, and (DME)1.6LiFSI-HFE are 2.29, 2.19, and 2.16 V, respectively.
Also, as shown in Figure S20b, the reduction peak in (DME)1.6LiTFSI-HFE is 2.22 V, higher than that of (DME)3LiFSI-HFE and lower than that of (DME)9LiFSI.

This reduction potential method is reasonable because the solvation energy aroused by the electrolyte to S8 (S8(s) →S8(l), ΔGsolvation) will increase the total free energy change (ΔGtotal = ΔG + ΔGsolvation) of the redox reaction, S8 + 2Li+ + 2e−→Li2S8.37,38 According to the Nernst equation, ΔG = −nFU, a higher ΔGsolvation would result in a higher ΔGtotal and a higher reduction potential of S8.

From the reduction potential in different electrolytes, we estimate the upper limit of reduction potential that enables the Li-S battery to work under a lean-electrolyte condition lies in the range of 2.16−2.19 V.
Once the reduction potential exceeds this limit, the solvation capability of the electrolyte is too high and is incapable of suppressing polysulfide dissolution effectively.

Note that the cathode area capacity in Figure 6I reaches 7.5 mAh cm−2 in the initial cycle, considering the electrolyte volume (VE = 2 μL mg−1 × 5 mg cm−2 = 10 μL cm−2), and 1 mAh cm−2 (5 μm in thickness) lithium metal only corresponds to 1.3 μL of the electrolyte (this calculation does not consider the loss of electrolyte in the dead spaces in Li-S coin cells).
Under such a lean-electrolyte condition, the Li-S battery suffers serious capacity fading due to the consumption of electrolyte in the anode.
The increased sulfur utilization under a lean-electrolyte condition certainly helps to improve the practical energy density (PED) of the Li-S battery.
In this work, an Ah-level Li- S pouch cell with critical parameters was demonstrated to validate the improvement of PED.

Figure 7a gives a schematic of the structure of the Li-S pouch cell assembled in this work, which contains two single-side-coated sulfur cathodes, four double-side-coated sulfur cathodes, and five pieces of lithium anode (single piece lithium: 200 μm, 40 mAh cm−2).
The cathode was prepared through a commonly used blade-casting method with commercial cheap raw materials according to our previous work,23 and the single-side sulfur loading is kept at 7 mg cm−2.
The porosity of the cathode is calculated to be 55% with a compacted density of 0.66 g S cm−3 (Figure 7c).
The pore volume of the S cathode is about 1.75, and 2.1 mL of the electrolyte was added to the pouch cell.
The N/P ratio is about 2 in the pouch cell.
Figure 7b gives the weight distribution of the components used to assemble the Li-S pouch cell (the weight of each component can be found in Table S1).
The lower part in Figure 7c is the Li-S pouch cell assembled in this work.

Figure 7d gives the voltage−capacity curve of the Li-S pouch cell tested under a lean-electrolyte condition of E/S = 1 μL mg−1, and the current density used here is 0.05C in the initial cycle and 0.1C in the following, and the test temperature is 30 °C.
It can be found that the capacity of the Li-S pouch cell can reach 2.3 Ah.
Under such a lean-electrolyte condition, the PED of Li-S pouch cell can achieve 589 Wh kg−1, surpassing state-of-the-art lithium-ion batteries and flooded electrolyte Li-S batteries.
Figure 7e gives the cycling performance of the Li-S pouch cell, which shows a serious capacity fade.

We found that the lithium metal anode was seriously pulverized during the cycle by disassembling the failed cell, which will undoubtedly increase the specific surface of the anode and thus aggravate the consumption of electrolyte.
At the same time, a large number of pores are generated after cycling, which consume a large amount of electrolyte, increasing the polarization at the Li anode side and leading to battery failure.

We have to admit that it is a great challenge to avoid the electrolyte consumption in the lithium−metal anode at such a high area capacity (10 mAh cm−2) and high current density without extra protection of the lithium−metal anode.

However, we still have the confidence that the electrolyte consumption can be alleviated either by electrolyte optimization or lithium anode protection in the near future, so as to enable a high practical energy density Li-S battery to work stably for dozens of cycles (e.g., 50 cycles ending up with 500 Wh kg−1). ■CONCLUSIONS In conclusion, we found that the real solubility of sulfide in the electrolyte is far more than the 6−7 MS reported in the literature by using an evaporation method to test the solubility, which could influence the viscosity of the electrolyte and eventually cause a gelation transition (where E/S is reduced to a certain extent by the liquid into a solid electrolyte), affecting the utilization efficiency of active substances and PGED of the Li-sulfur battery.

More importantly, we demonstrated that the sulfur cathode can perform electrochemical reactions independently of the dissolution of polysulfide and operate under an ultralow electrolyte condition (E/S = 1 μL mg−1) by reducing the solvation capacity of the electrolyte, which can effectively delay the gelation transition and improve the electrochemical performance of Li-sulfur batteries under leanelectrolyte conditions.

Specifically, high sulfur utilizations of 96% (1600 mAh g−1) and 78% (1300 mAh g−1) are reached in electrolytes as lean as E/S = 2 and 1 μL mg−1 Li-S coin cells, respetively, even paired against a high-sulfur-loading cathode (5 mg cm−2).

Furthermore, a Li-S pouch cell (with dimensions of 5.0 cm × 6.0 cm, sulfur loading of 7 mg cm−2, and 1× lithium excess) was constructed with E/S = 1 μL mg−1 and it turns out that the actual energy density of the Li-S battery can reach 589 Wh kg−1, doubling that of state-of-the-art LIBs. ■ASSOCIATED CONTENT * sı Supporting Information The Supporting Information is available free of charge at https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acsami.2c10906.
